extracted.intended_audience: olympiad and pre-olympiad students (math contest participants and learners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, precise, and correct mathematical proofs aimed at olympiad and pre-olympiad students; covers fundamental principles, common proof methods, and practice recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision
rubrics_metrics.description: "A single word can change the intended meaning of a proof, so it is best to be as precise as possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose wording carefully so statements convey exactly what is intended; avoid ambiguous or imprecise terms that could alter meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct from precision; the proof must say true things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every asserted statement is correct and justified; do not include false or unchecked claims even if phrased precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with the reader in mind (e.g., contest graders or peers); organize steps logically and use notation/phrasing appropriate for the audience to make reasoning easy to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: "Proofs require the ability to think abstractly, that is, universally" — not just for the example at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to prove general statements or explain why an argument works in all relevant cases rather than only demonstrating a single instance; favor universal reasoning over ad hoc examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality (formal vs. informal)
rubrics_metrics.description: University-level mathematicians do not accept informal proofs as valid; informal proofs serve as teaching tools at best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For contest/advanced-level work present proofs with sufficient rigor and formal structure; informal intuition is useful for discovery but should be converted into a valid formal argument for submission or publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-column format (geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-column format: standard for early geometry proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-column style where appropriate (especially in early geometry education) to pair statements with justifications, but adapt format to contest or reader expectations at higher levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction / induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction/induction: one of two predominant formal methods at advanced levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructive techniques or mathematical induction where appropriate to build objects or prove statements for all natural numbers/cases; present base cases and inductive steps clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradiction: the other major formal method, requiring derivation of a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using contradiction, state the negation of the desired conclusion, derive a logical contradiction, and conclude the original statement holds; make the contradiction explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice: use AoPS forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AoPS forums to practice writing solutions with clarity and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post solutions to get feedback and iterate on clarity and completeness; treat forum practice as a way to hone presentation skills under peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice: read other students' solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Read other students' solutions to identify improvements in your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study different solution styles and approaches to learn clearer exposition, alternative methods, and common pitfalls to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept constructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to feedback on style, rigor, and clarity; use critiques to refine proofs rather than defending informal or unclear reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribute to mathematical wikis
rubrics_metrics.description: Contribute to mathematical wikis to develop precise mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing for reference resources forces precision and clear exposition; explain reasoning fully so others can follow and learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Olympiad problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Study Olympiad problems for advanced practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use past contest problems to practice crafting concise, rigorous proofs under contest-style constraints and to internalize common techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition rubric weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: For competition math, the rubric is heavily weighted toward precision + universality + correctness; literary value is largely orthogonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize mathematically precise, universally applicable, and correct arguments over stylistic flourish; readability matters, but literary elegance is secondary to correctness and generality in contest grading.
